A_target.statement:
Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a [[Definition:Probability Space|probability space]] and $A_1, \ldots, A_n \in \Sigma$.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \map \Pr {\bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_i} \le \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map \Pr {A_i}$

B_source.statement:
Let $\mu$ be a [[Definition:Measure (Measure Theory)|measure]] and $E_1, E_2, \ldots$ measurable.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \map \mu {\bigcup_i E_i} \le \sum_i \map \mu {E_i}$

validity_conditions: A probability measure is a measure (with total mass 1), so subadditivity applies directly.
No limit or extra hypothesis is needed; this is a direct instantiation, hence specialization rather than generalization.
proof_plan: By [[Measure is Countably Subadditive]], every measure is countably subadditive.
Take $\mu = \Pr$, $E_i = A_i$ for $i \le n$ and $E_i = \O$ for $i > n$.
